neurological_exam.mental_status: Alert and fully oriented. MoCA 21/30 with losses in trail-making, cube, clock, digit span backwards, serial sevens and delayed recall (1/5 unaided, 2/5 with cueing, 3/5 recognition). Notably poor at copying and at drawing a plan, which he volunteers is 'the thing an architect cannot lose'.
neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: Pupils equal and reactive. Extraocular movements full. Visual fields full. Face symmetric. Speech fluent.

neurological_exam.sensory: Reduced pinprick in the left L5 dermatome, long-standing after the fusion.

neurological_exam.additional: No frontal release signs. No parkinsonian features. Pulse regular at 68.

patient.chief_complaint: Three years of visuospatial and memory difficulty in an architect, with a heavy white matter burden on a scan done for headache
patient.history_present_illness: Mr. Claudio Ferri is a 70-year-old retired architect who was referred after an MRI performed for headache showed extensive white matter change. He and his wife describe three years of difficulty that began with drawing and spatial tasks: he could no longer sketch a floor plan to scale, made errors reading his own old drawings, and gave up a consultancy he had continued into retirement. Memory difficulty followed: he forgets conversations and cannot retain a message, and his wife says that reminding him of the context does not help. He has become mildly slower but she is emphatic that slowness is not the problem — the problem is that he 'cannot see how things fit together' and does not remember. There have been no abrupt events, no weakness, no speech disturbance and no gait change. He has hypertension of eighteen years, treated, and well-adhered CPAP for sleep apnoea. There is no family history of dementia. He declines any spinal procedure after a difficult lumbar fusion, and refuses a lumbar puncture when it is offered. There are no hallucinations, no fluctuation and no dream enactment.

additional_observations: Two findings compete for the diagnosis: a Fazekas 3 confluent white matter burden with two lacunes, and marked posterior cortical atrophy with Scheltens 2 medial temporal atrophy
The posterior atrophy pattern is not produced by small-vessel disease and matches the visuospatial-led clinical syndrome
SWI shows no microbleeds and no cortical superficial siderosis, and there is no cortical infarct
The white matter burden is strikingly severe for a treated hypertensive of 70 and is the reason for the referral
mri.impression: Severe confluent small-vessel disease (Fazekas 3, two lacunes) coexisting with marked posterior cortical atrophy and moderate medial temporal atrophy. The atrophy pattern, not the white matter burden, matches the clinical syndrome.

labs.interpretation: LDL 82 mg/dL on rosuvastatin is close to target. TSH, B12, folate, RPR and HIV are normal or negative. There is no reversible cause and no metabolic contributor.

advanced_imaging.impression: Strongly positive amyloid PET with posterior predominance. Amyloid pathology is established and its distribution matches the visuospatial-led clinical syndrome. With a Fazekas 3 white matter burden also present, the diagnosis is mixed Alzheimer and vascular dementia.

quantitative_data.pattern: posterior cortical: visuospatial and storage memory failure with processing speed preserved
quantitative_data.dissociation: processing speed at the 26th percentile against visuospatial function at the 1st-3rd

specialized_test.impression: The dissociation is the finding: visuospatial and constructional performance is at the 1st-3rd percentile and recognition memory at the 8th, while processing speed and fluency are within normal limits. Subcortical small-vessel disease produces the opposite dissociation — slowed processing with preserved posterior cortical function — so the Fazekas 3 burden is not the driver of this syndrome.

This is the wrong shape for subcortical small-vessel disease, in which slowing and executive failure lead and recall is cue-responsive, and it points to a posteriorly weighted degenerative process despite the striking white matter burden.

vascular_cognitive_impairment.query: vascular cognitive impairment diagnostic criteria and secondary prevention

results.title: Diagnostic criteria for vascular cognitive disorders: a VASCOG statement
results.authors: Sachdev P, Kalaria R, O'Brien J, et al.
results.summary: Requires a cognitive syndrome documented on a validated instrument plus imaging or temporal evidence that cerebrovascular disease accounts for it.

results.title: Neuroimaging standards for research into small vessel disease (STRIVE-2)
results.authors: Duering M, Biessels GJ, Brodtmann A, et al.
results.summary: Defines and standardises the reporting of white matter hyperintensity, lacunes, microbleeds, perivascular spaces and cortical superficial siderosis.

vascular_cognitive_impairment.summary: No disease-modifying therapy exists for vascular cognitive impairment; management is control of the vascular risk factors, secondary prevention matched to the mechanism, review of the anticholinergic burden, and treatment of coexisting Alzheimer pathology where biomarkers support it.

medication_review.proposed: review of the current medication list for anticholinergic burden
warnings: Anticholinergic load is a reversible contributor to cognitive impairment in this population and should be quantified before any new prescription.
medication_review.summary: No prohibitive interaction identified within the current list.

ground_truth.primary_diagnosis: Mixed Alzheimer and vascular dementia, with a posterior-predominant Alzheimer syndrome as the leading pathology and severe coexisting small-vessel disease

differential.key_features: This is what the Fazekas 3 burden invites and it is the reason for referral, but the cognitive dissociation runs the wrong way — visuospatial function at the 1st percentile with processing speed at the 26th — and amyloid PET is strongly positive with a posterior predominance

differential.diagnosis: Posterior cortical atrophy (visual variant of Alzheimer's disease)
differential.key_features: The visuospatial-led presentation with posterior atrophy and positive amyloid fits this phenotype closely; it is a variant of the Alzheimer component rather than an alternative to it, and the coexisting severe vascular burden must still be treated
Visuospatial failure is prominent in DLB, but there are no hallucinations, no fluctuation, no parkinsonism and no dream enactment
CPAP adherence is good and the profile is not the attentional pattern of untreated apnoea
No limb apraxia to command, no alien limb, no asymmetric rigidity or myoclonus

optimal_actions.action: Obtain a collateral history from an informant who sees the patient daily: the shape of the decline (abrupt, stepwise or gradual), whether any step can be dated to a cerebrovascular event, and which instrumental activities have been lost
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Three years of insidious decline led by visuospatial and then amnestic failure, with slowness a minor feature, no dateable events and no family history — a degenerative rather than a stepwise course despite a heavy white matter burden

optimal_actions.action: Perform a validated bedside cognitive assessment and record the per-domain profile and whether delayed recall improves with cueing
optimal_actions.expected_finding: MoCA 21/30 with a visuospatial-led, storage-weighted profile and only mild slowing — the wrong shape for a subcortical vascular syndrome

optimal_actions.action: Order the reversible-cause screen and the vascular-risk assays that will be treated (CBC, CMP, TSH, B12, folate, RPR, HIV, HbA1c, lipid panel)
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Reversible causes excluded; vascular risk factors reasonably controlled, with no metabolic contributor to the syndrome

optimal_actions.action: Obtain brain MRI reported in STRIVE-2 terms — FLAIR for white matter hyperintensity with a Fazekas grade, T1/T2 for lacunes, DWI to establish that the lesions are chronic, and SWI for microbleeds and cortical superficial siderosis — together with the medial temporal atrophy grade
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Fazekas 3 confluent white matter change with two lacunes alongside marked posterior cortical atrophy (Koedam 2-3) and Scheltens 2 medial temporal atrophy

optimal_actions.action: Order formal multi-domain neuropsychological testing to settle the executive-versus-amnestic attribution and to document a baseline for follow-up
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Visuospatial-led profile with storage-type memory failure and only mild executive slowing — a posterior cortical rather than subcortical pattern

optimal_actions.action: Obtain amyloid PET where coexisting Alzheimer pathology is the specific question and CSF sampling is declined or unavailable
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Positive cortical amyloid retention with a posterior predominance — Alzheimer pathology established without a lumbar puncture, which the patient refuses after his spinal surgery

optimal_actions.action: Obtain FDG-PET to separate a temporoparietal Alzheimer pattern from the patchy multifocal hypometabolism that follows white matter lesions
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Posterior parietal and precuneus hypometabolism disproportionate to the white matter lesion distribution — the metabolic pattern follows the cortex, not the lesions

optimal_actions.action: Confirm the diagnostic criteria applied and the current secondary-prevention targets against the guidelines
optimal_actions.expected_finding: VASCOG 2014 criteria and the 2021 AHA/ASA secondary prevention targets confirmed

optimal_actions.action: Review the medication list for anticholinergic burden and for the interaction between antithrombotic choice and the microbleed burden before prescribing
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Anticholinergic contributors identified and the antithrombotic choice reconciled with the imaging burden

optimal_actions.action: Establish the Alzheimer component with amyloid PET rather than the lumbar puncture the patient refuses, start a cholinesterase inhibitor, treat the severe vascular burden in its own right with blood pressure below 130 mmHg systolic and LDL below 70 mg/dL, maintain CPAP adherence, arrange occupational therapy for the visuospatial deficit including a formal driving assessment despite the absence of informant concern, and review the duloxetine for cognitive burden
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Alzheimer component established non-invasively and treated, severe vascular burden treated in parallel, visuospatial deficit assessed for driving safety, and the analgesic regimen reviewed

optimal_actions.action: Disclose the diagnosis and its mechanism to the patient and the informant, and address driving, medication management, finances, advance care planning and caregiver support
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Patient and informant engaged in care planning; safety domains addressed

useless_tools.rationale: EEG has no diagnostic role in vascular cognitive impairment; it belongs to the differential of a rapidly progressive or fluctuating course (Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease, non-convulsive status, toxic-metabolic encephalopathy), none of which is present here

A presynaptic dopaminergic study answers the Lewy-body question, not the vascular one, and there is no spontaneous parkinsonism, no fluctuating cognition with hallucinations and no REM sleep behaviour disorder
Cardiac sympathetic imaging is a test for dementia with Lewy bodies and for autonomic failure; it says nothing about cerebrovascular disease

An untargeted paraneoplastic or autoimmune-encephalitis battery in a chronic stepwise decline with a hypertensive imaging burden is the archetypal expensive miss; the indication for those assays is a subacute multidomain syndrome
The MRI already obtained answers everything a CT could and more: CT cannot show microbleeds or cortical superficial siderosis, so it cannot grade the vascular burden this diagnosis rests on
There is no embolic lesion pattern to explain: the burden here is small-vessel, and a structural cardioembolic source would not account for it
Prolonged rhythm monitoring is for an unexplained embolic infarct pattern; in pure small-vessel disease it changes nothing about the diagnosis or the treatment

sequence_constraints.reason: Document the cognitive deficit before attributing it: imaging read without a cognitive profile invites over-attribution of incidental white matter change

critical_actions: Match the cognitive profile to the pathology rather than to the most striking imaging finding
Test visuospatial function and processing speed separately, because the direction of the dissociation identifies the leading pathology
Test recognition memory to establish storage failure
Read the MRI for the atrophy pattern as well as the white matter burden, including a posterior atrophy score
Choose a biomarker route the patient will accept where a lumbar puncture is refused
Treat the coexisting severe vascular burden even though it is not the leading pathology
Assess driving formally when visuospatial function is at the 1st percentile, even without informant concern
contraindicated_actions: Do not diagnose vascular dementia from a Fazekas 3 burden when the cognitive dissociation points the other way
Do not pursue a lumbar puncture in a patient who explicitly refuses spinal procedures when amyloid PET answers the same question
Do not omit vascular risk-factor treatment because the leading pathology is degenerative
Do not rely on the absence of informant concern to clear driving when visuospatial testing is at the 1st percentile
Do not prescribe anticholinergic medications alongside a cholinesterase inhibitor
key_reasoning_points: The direction of the cognitive dissociation identifies the pathology: subcortical vascular disease slows processing while sparing posterior cortical function, and this patient shows the reverse
A striking white matter burden is not evidence of the mechanism of a cognitive syndrome whose shape does not fit it — imaging severity and clinical relevance are different questions
The FDG pattern adds an independent argument: hypometabolism follows the posterior cortex rather than the extent of the white matter lesions
Amyloid PET substitutes for CSF where a patient refuses a lumbar puncture, and the refusal is a legitimate clinical constraint rather than an obstacle to be argued away
The vascular burden still requires treatment even when it is not the leading pathology, because it accelerates the degenerative decline

red_herrings.data_point: A Fazekas 3 white matter burden that prompted the referral
red_herrings.intended_effect: Frames the whole assessment as vascular dementia, which is also how the referral was written
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: The cognitive dissociation runs the wrong way for a subcortical syndrome — visuospatial function at the 1st percentile with normal processing speed — and amyloid PET is strongly positive with posterior predominance

red_herrings.intended_effect: Offers an alternative explanation for cognitive impairment with a heavy white matter burden
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: CPAP adherence is good and the profile is visuospatial and amnestic rather than the attentional pattern of untreated apnoea

key_educational_points: The direction of a cognitive dissociation identifies the pathology more reliably than the severity of an imaging finding
Posterior cortical atrophy scores belong in the report of a dementia MRI alongside the white matter grade
FDG hypometabolism that does not follow the white matter lesions argues against a vascular mechanism
A refused lumbar puncture is a reason to use amyloid PET, not a reason to abandon biomarkers
